claim: Maneuverability is defined as the ability of an animal to change the speed and direction of movement.
source: The ability of an animal to change the speed and direction of movement, defined as maneuverability (Dudley, 2002), can determine its success at avoiding predators, obtaining food, and performing other behaviors that determine the margin between life and death (Webb, 1976; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001; Walker et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dudley, 2002.

claim: Maneuverability can determine an animal's success at avoiding predators, obtaining food, and performing other behaviors that determine the margin between life and death.
source: The ability of an animal to change the speed and direction of movement, defined as maneuverability (Dudley, 2002), can determine its success at avoiding predators, obtaining food, and performing other behaviors that determine the margin between life and death (Webb, 1976; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001; Walker et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Webb, 1976; Hedenström and Rosén, 2001; Walker et al., 2005.

claim: Maneuverability is one of the most important but least understood aspects of animal locomotion.
source: Maneuverability is therefore one of the most important but least understood aspects of animal locomotion.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the context that most biomechanical research has focused on brief or steady state movements rather than maneuverability.

claim: There are both intrinsic and facultative influences on maneuvering performance in powered flight.
source: Warrick and coworkers (Warrick et al., 1988; Warrick and Dial, 1998) proposed that there are both intrinsic and facultative influences on maneuvering performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Warrick et al., 1988 and Warrick and Dial, 1998.

claim: Intrinsic maneuverability for animals that perform powered flight is defined by the physical limitations imposed by morphology.
source: For animals that perform powered flight, intrinsic maneuverability is defined by the physical limitations imposed by morphology (Norberg and Rayner, 1987), but excess muscle capacity should allow them to facultatively overcome the costs of suboptimal morphology, achieving higher levels of performance by sacrificing efficiency.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Norberg and Rayner, 1987.

claim: Excess muscle capacity should allow animals to facultatively overcome the costs of suboptimal morphology, achieving higher levels of performance by sacrificing efficiency.
source: For animals that perform powered flight, intrinsic maneuverability is defined by the physical limitations imposed by morphology (Norberg and Rayner, 1987), but excess muscle capacity should allow them to facultatively overcome the costs of suboptimal morphology, achieving higher levels of performance by sacrificing efficiency.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the role of excess muscle capacity.

claim: The hypothesis that excess muscle capacity allows animals to overcome costs of suboptimal morphology has never been tested explicitly.
source: Although compelling, this hypothesis has never been tested explicitly.
evidence: The claim is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Wing area and aspect ratio have significant and well known effects on the aerodynamics of flight in animals.
source: Wing area and aspect ratio have significant and well known effects on the aerodynamics of flight in animals (Pennycuick, 1975; Kruyt et al., 2014; 2015), and should affect maneuvering performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pennycuick, 1975; Kruyt et al., 2014; 2015.

claim: Wing area and aspect ratio should affect maneuvering performance.
source: Wing area and aspect ratio have significant and well known effects on the aerodynamics of flight in animals (Pennycuick, 1975; Kruyt et al., 2014; 2015), and should affect maneuvering performance.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the known effects of wing morphology on aerodynamics.

claim: Wing morphology influences flight efficiency.
source: Wing morphology influences flight efficiency (Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975), ecological roles (Feinsinger, 1976; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Warrick, 1998) and competitive ability (Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Feinsinger et al., 1979; Altshuler, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975.

claim: Wing morphology influences ecological roles.
source: Wing morphology influences flight efficiency (Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975), ecological roles (Feinsinger, 1976; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Warrick, 1998) and competitive ability (Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Feinsinger et al., 1979; Altshuler, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feinsinger, 1976; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Warrick, 1998.

claim: Wing morphology influences competitive ability.
source: Wing morphology influences flight efficiency (Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975), ecological roles (Feinsinger, 1976; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Warrick, 1998) and competitive ability (Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Feinsinger et al., 1979; Altshuler, 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Feinsinger et al., 1979; Altshuler, 2006.

claim: Less is known about how individual variation in wing morphology influences performance, especially with respect to maneuverability.
source: Because these previous studies focused on species and gender comparisons, less is known about how individual variation in wing morphology influences performance, especially with respect to maneuverability.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the focus of previous studies.

claim: Different wing sizes and shapes can be favored depending on the specific maneuver performed.
source: One complication is that different wing sizes and shapes can be favored depending on the specific maneuver performed, e.g., yaw versus banked turns.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the relationship between wing morphology and different types of maneuvers.

claim: It is unclear if the requirements for maneuvering exert strong selection on wing morphology given the diversity of flight behaviors.
source: Given the diversity of flight behaviors, it is unclear if the requirements for maneuvering exert strong selection on wing morphology.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about selection pressures.

claim: Muscle capacity affects the maximum aerodynamic force a flying animal can produce.
source: Muscle capacity affects the maximum aerodynamic force a flying animal can produce.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about muscle function.

claim: Aerodynamic force can be directed for performing maneuvers that require greater output than the minimum requirements for flight.
source: Aerodynamic force can be directed for performing maneuvers that require greater output than the minimum requirements for flight.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about how aerodynamic force is used.

claim: Excess muscle capacity can be used to compensate for anatomical or spatial constraints on wing movement.
source: Excess muscle capacity can also be used to compensate for anatomical or spatial constraints on wing movement (Warrick, 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Warrick, 1998.

claim: Forward flight at the fastest speeds recorded in a wind tunnel requires about 20% more metabolic input than hovering flight.
source: Considering hovering flight as the point of comparison, forward flight at the fastest speeds recorded in a wind tunnel requires about 20% more metabolic (Clark and Dudley, 2010) and myoelectric input (Tobalske et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Clark and Dudley, 2010.

claim: Forward flight at the fastest speeds recorded in a wind tunnel requires about 20% more myoelectric input than hovering flight.
source: Considering hovering flight as the point of comparison, forward flight at the fastest speeds recorded in a wind tunnel requires about 20% more metabolic (Clark and Dudley, 2010) and myoelectric input (Tobalske et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tobalske et al., 2010.

claim: Hovering in hypodense air requires ~40% higher mechanical power output compared to hovering in normal air.
source: These experiments revealed that hovering in hypodense air requires ~40% higher mechanical power output (Chai and Dudley, 1995) and ~60% higher spatial recruitment of muscle fibers, as measured by the spike amplitude of the electromyogram recordings (Altshuler et al., 2010b), in comparison to hovering in normal air.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chai and Dudley, 1995.

claim: Hovering in hypodense air requires ~60% higher spatial recruitment of muscle fibers compared to hovering in normal air.
source: These experiments revealed that hovering in hypodense air requires ~40% higher mechanical power output (Chai and Dudley, 1995) and ~60% higher spatial recruitment of muscle fibers, as measured by the spike amplitude of the electromyogram recordings (Altshuler et al., 2010b), in comparison to hovering in normal air.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Altshuler et al., 2010b.

claim: Maximum load lifting is the most expensive flight behavior studied to date in hummingbirds.
source: By far the most expensive flight behavior studied to date in hummingbirds is maximum load lifting, which requires 200–400% more mechanical power output (Chai et al., 1997; Chai and Millard, 1997; Altshuler et al., 2010a), about 200% more spatial recruitment (EMG spike amplitude), and 150% more temporal recruitment (EMG spike frequency) (Altshuler et al., 2010b) compared to hovering.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chai et al., 1997; Chai and Millard, 1997; Altshuler et al., 2010a; Altshuler et al., 2010b.

claim: Maximum load lifting requires 200–400% more mechanical power output compared to hovering.
source: By far the most expensive flight behavior studied to date in hummingbirds is maximum load lifting, which requires 200–400% more mechanical power output (Chai et al., 1997; Chai and Millard, 1997; Altshuler et al., 2010a), about 200% more spatial recruitment (EMG spike amplitude), and 150% more temporal recruitment (EMG spike frequency) (Altshuler et al., 2010b) compared to hovering.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chai et al., 1997; Chai and Millard, 1997; Altshuler et al., 2010a.

claim: Maximum load lifting requires about 200% more spatial recruitment (EMG spike amplitude) compared to hovering.
source: By far the most expensive flight behavior studied to date in hummingbirds is maximum load lifting, which requires 200–400% more mechanical power output (Chai et al., 1997; Chai and Millard, 1997; Altshuler et al., 2010a), about 200% more spatial recruitment (EMG spike amplitude), and 150% more temporal recruitment (EMG spike frequency) (Altshuler et al., 2010b) compared to hovering.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Altshuler et al., 2010b.

claim: Maximum load lifting requires 150% more temporal recruitment (EMG spike frequency) compared to hovering.
source: By far the most expensive flight behavior studied to date in hummingbirds is maximum load lifting, which requires 200–400% more mechanical power output (Chai et al., 1997; Chai and Millard, 1997; Altshuler et al., 2010a), about 200% more spatial recruitment (EMG spike amplitude), and 150% more temporal recruitment (EMG spike frequency) (Altshuler et al., 2010b) compared to hovering.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Altshuler et al., 2010b.

claim: Maximum load lifting is a transient behavior that uses the bird's natural escape response to measure burst power output.
source: Maximum load lifting is a transient behavior that uses the bird's natural escape response to measure burst power output.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the load lifting assay.

claim: The load lifting assay provides the maximum muscle capacity that has been measured in hummingbirds.
source: Thus, it is not surprising that this assay provides the maximum muscle capacity that has been measured in hummingbirds.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the nature of the load lifting assay.

claim: Maximum burst muscle capacity is related to hummingbird evolutionary ecology.
source: Studies using the load lifting assay have revealed that maximum burst muscle capacity is related to hummingbird evolutionary ecology.
evidence: The claim is supported by inference from studies using the load lifting assay.

claim: Ecological role is more strongly related to load lifting ability than morphological parameters such as wing loading.
source: Altshuler and coworkers (Altshuler et al., 2004b; Altshuler, 2006) demonstrated that ecological role is more strongly related to load lifting ability than morphological parameters such as wing loading.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Altshuler et al., 2004b and Altshuler, 2006.

claim: Load lifting ability is associated with species- and gender-specific competitive ability at different elevations.
source: Load lifting ability is also associated with species- and gender-specific competitive ability at different elevations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous studies.

claim: The relationship between maximum muscle capacity and competitive ability may be mediated through maneuvering performance.
source: Altshuler (Altshuler, 2006) suggested that the relationship between maximum muscle capacity and competitive ability may be mediated through maneuvering performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Altshuler, 2006 and represents a hypothesis.

claim: Unconstrained maneuvering performance of birds, including hummingbirds, has recently been quantified in the field without individual identification.
source: Unconstrained maneuvering performance of birds, including hummingbirds, has recently been quantified in the field without individual identification (Shelton et al., 2014; Sholtis et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Shelton et al., 2014 and Sholtis et al., 2015.

claim: Individual identification and large sample sizes are required to examine sources of within-species variation in maneuvering performance.
source: Although field studies are valuable for quantifying average species performance, individual identification and large sample sizes are required to examine sources of within-species variation.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about methodological requirements.

claim: Flight maneuvers in a chamber are not expected to be the same as outdoors, and may have lower velocities and accelerations.
source: Flight maneuvers in a chamber are not expected to be the same as outdoors, and may have lower velocities and accelerations.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the effects of chamber constraints.

claim: The benefit of using a flight chamber is that a large number of measurements from the same individuals can be combined with other data to examine how variation in the observed maneuvers is influenced by individual morphology and muscle capacity.
source: The benefit of this approach is that a large number of measurements from the same individuals can be combined with other data to examine how variation in the observed maneuvers is influenced by individual morphology and muscle capacity.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about the advantages of the chamber approach.

claim: The study used an automated tracking system to record flight sequences from 20 Anna's hummingbirds flying solo and in competition in a large chamber.
source: We used an automated tracking system to record flight sequences from 20 Anna's hummingbirds flying solo and in competition in a large chamber.
evidence: The claim is supported by the description of the experimental methods.

claim: Burst muscle capacity predicted most performance metrics in Anna's hummingbirds.
source: We found that burst muscle capacity predicted most performance metrics.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Hummingbirds with higher burst capacity flew with faster velocities, accelerations, and rotations.
source: Hummingbirds with higher burst capacity flew with faster velocities, accelerations, and rotations, and they used more demanding complex turns.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Hummingbirds with higher burst capacity used more demanding complex turns.
source: Hummingbirds with higher burst capacity flew with faster velocities, accelerations, and rotations, and they used more demanding complex turns.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Body mass did not predict variation in maneuvering performance.
source: In contrast, body mass did not predict variation in maneuvering performance, and wing morphology predicted only the use of arcing turns and high centripetal accelerations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Wing morphology predicted only the use of arcing turns and high centripetal accelerations.
source: In contrast, body mass did not predict variation in maneuvering performance, and wing morphology predicted only the use of arcing turns and high centripetal accelerations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Burst muscle capacity is a key predictor of maneuverability.
source: Collectively, our results indicate that burst muscle capacity is a key predictor of maneuverability.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in the study.

claim: Translational velocity and acceleration were calculated by taking the first and second derivatives of an interpolation spline fit to the body position data.
source: Translational velocity and acceleration were calculated by taking the first and second derivatives of an interpolation spline fit to the body position data (splev and splrep functions, Scientific Python).
evidence: The claim describes the data processing methods used in the study.

claim: The velocities and accelerations were split into vertical and horizontal components.
source: The velocities and accelerations were split into vertical and horizontal components.
evidence: The claim describes the data processing methods used in the study.

claim: The body orientation vector was represented in spherical coordinates as azimuth and pitch angles.
source: The body orientation vector was represented in spherical coordinates as azimuth and pitch angles.
evidence: The claim describes the data processing methods used in the study.

claim: A global coordinate system was used instead of a body axis-centered coordinate system because the video tracking system did not allow a measurement of body roll.
source: Because the video tracking system did not allow a measurement of body roll, we decided to use a global coordinate system instead of a body axis-centered coordinate system.
evidence: The claim describes a methodological decision based on technical limitations.

claim: Pitch is a global measure defined relative to the horizontal plane.
source: In our frame of reference, pitch is a global measure defined relative to the horizontal plane.
evidence: The claim describes the coordinate system used in the study.

claim: Heading was calculated as the instantaneous direction of the horizontal translation velocity.
source: Heading was calculated as the instantaneous direction of the horizontal translation velocity, and the heading velocity was calculated as the derivative of heading.
evidence: The claim describes the data processing methods used in the study.

claim: Ten stereotyped maneuvers were identified that were independent of time and distance scales.
source: We then used the velocity, acceleration, and orientation data to search for a series of ten stereotyped maneuvers that were independent of time and distance scales (Figure 1b).
evidence: The claim describes the maneuver classification approach used in the study.

claim: The ten maneuvers are not meant to be mutually exclusive, exhaustive, or to divide the entire filming session into a set of discrete behaviors.
source: These ten maneuvers are not meant to be mutually exclusive, exhaustive, or to divide the entire filming session into a set of discrete behaviors, but are instead intended to extract simple measurements that can be used as an assay for maneuvering performance.
evidence: The claim clarifies the purpose and limitations of the maneuver classification.

claim: A large sample of values was obtained for each maneuvering performance metric.
source: A large sample of values was obtained for each maneuvering performance metric (Table 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data presented in Table 3.

claim: All performance metrics based on total and horizontal linear accelerations and complex turns were highly repeatable, with >80% of the variation in these metrics attributable to differences among individuals.
source: All performance metrics based on total and horizontal linear accelerations and complex turns were highly repeatable, with >80% of the variation in these metrics attributable to differences among individuals (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the repeatability analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: The rotational performance metrics and the percent of turns that were pitch-roll turns were moderately repeatable, with 40–70% of the variation in these metrics attributable to among-individual differences.
source: The rotational performance metrics and the percent of turns that were pitch-roll turns were moderately repeatable, with 40–70% of the variation in these metrics attributable to among-individual differences.
evidence: The claim is supported by the repeatability analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: The vertical accelerations were not repeatable, as the 95% confidence intervals for repeatability of these metrics overlapped zero.
source: The vertical accelerations were not repeatable, as the 95% confidence intervals for repeatability of these metrics overlapped zero.
evidence: The claim is supported by the repeatability analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: Burst muscle capacity was an important predictor for most of the maneuvering performance metrics.
source: Burst muscle capacity was an important predictor for most of the maneuvering performance metrics.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Birds that lifted more weight (accounting for their wing morphology) tended to accelerate and decelerate faster.
source: Birds that lifted more weight (accounting for their wing morphology) tended to accelerate and decelerate faster, and they tended to perform maneuvers with higher velocity (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Birds that lifted more weight tended to perform maneuvers with higher velocity.
source: Birds that lifted more weight (accounting for their wing morphology) tended to accelerate and decelerate faster, and they tended to perform maneuvers with higher velocity (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Burst muscle capacity was not an important determinant of vertical acceleration and deceleration.
source: However, burst muscle capacity was not an important determinant of vertical acceleration and deceleration, as candidate models including burst performance as a predictor were not supported.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Birds that lifted more weight executed pitch-up and pitch-down maneuvers with higher rotational velocities.
source: Birds that lifted more weight also executed pitch-up and pitch-down maneuvers with higher rotational velocities.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis.

claim: Burst capacity was not a strong determinant of yaw performance.
source: Burst capacity was not a strong determinant of yaw performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Yaw velocity was somewhat positively related to burst capacity, but candidate models of yaw velocity that included burst as a predictor were not well supported.
source: Although yaw velocity was somewhat positively related to burst capacity (Figure 4), candidate models of yaw velocity that included burst as a predictor were not well supported.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 4 and Table 4.

claim: Birds with higher burst muscle capacity executed faster, larger radius arcing turns.
source: Birds that lifted more weight for their wing morphology tended to execute faster, larger radius arcing turns (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: The centripetal acceleration of arcing turns was not associated with burst capacity.
source: However, the centripetal acceleration of arcing turns was not associated with burst capacity.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Hummingbirds with higher load lifting capacity executed pitch-roll turns in less time.
source: Hummingbirds with higher load lifting capacity executed pitch-roll turns in less time.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis.

claim: Burst capacity was not a strong determinant of heading change during pitch-roll turns.
source: Burst capacity was not a strong determinant of heading change during pitch-roll turns.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Birds with higher burst muscle capacity used pitch-roll turns for proportionately more of their heading changes.
source: Lastly, birds with higher burst muscle capacity used pitch-roll turns for proportionately more of their heading changes.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis.

claim: Wing aspect ratio was an important predictor for centripetal acceleration and the percent of direction changes that were pitch-roll turns.
source: Wing morphology, specifically the aspect ratio, was an important predictor for two performance metrics: centripetal acceleration and the percent of direction changes that were pitch-roll turns (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Figure 5 and Table 4.

claim: Hummingbirds with long, narrow wings tended to perform arcing turns with higher centripetal accelerations, relative to birds with short, wide wings.
source: Hummingbirds with long, narrow wings tended to perform arcing turns with higher centripetal accelerations, relative to birds with short, wide wings.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: Birds with higher aspect ratio wings used proportionately more arcing turns than birds with low aspect ratio wings.
source: Birds with higher aspect ratio wings also used proportionately more arcing turns than birds with low aspect ratio wings.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: For every performance metric in Table 4, the coefficient estimate for body mass had confidence intervals that broadly overlapped zero.
source: However, for every performance metric in Table 4, the coefficient estimate for body mass had confidence intervals that broadly overlapped zero.
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Competitor presence did not have a substantial effect on many of the performance metrics.
source: We did not detect a substantial effect of competitor presence on many of the performance metrics (Table 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Table 4.

claim: Birds performed maneuvers with lower acceleration (–0.46 m/s2 difference on average) in the presence of a competitor, relative to solo flight.
source: Specifically, birds performed maneuvers with lower acceleration (–0.46 m/s2 difference on average) and lower deceleration (–0.47 m/s2) in the presence of a competitor, relative to solo flight (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Birds performed maneuvers with lower deceleration (–0.47 m/s2) in the presence of a competitor, relative to solo flight.
source: Specifically, birds performed maneuvers with lower acceleration (–0.46 m/s2 difference on average) and lower deceleration (–0.47 m/s2) in the presence of a competitor, relative to solo flight (Figure 6a,b).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Pitch-down velocity increased during competition (0.06 rev/s difference on average).
source: One metric, pitch-down velocity (Figure 6c), did increase during competition as predicted (0.06 rev/s difference on average).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Birds used proportionately more arcing turns in the presence of a competitor.
source: We had no prediction for how competition would influence the relative use of pitch-roll and arcing turns, but found that birds used proportionately more arcing turns in the presence of a competitor (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: 35% of direction changes were arcing turns on average (and 65% pitch-roll) when a competitor was present.
source: Specifically, 35% of direction changes were arcing turns on average (and 65% pitch-roll) when a competitor was present, whereas during solo flight, only 23% of direction changes were arcing turns (and 77% pitch-roll) on average.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis.

claim: During solo flight, only 23% of direction changes were arcing turns (and 77% pitch-roll) on average.
source: Specifically, 35% of direction changes were arcing turns on average (and 65% pitch-roll) when a competitor was present, whereas during solo flight, only 23% of direction changes were arcing turns (and 77% pitch-roll) on average.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis.

claim: The values for velocity and acceleration in this study are considerably lower than field studies, likely because of cage size.
source: Our values for velocity and acceleration are considerably lower than either of the field studies, likely because of cage size.
evidence: The claim is based on inference comparing the study results to field studies.

claim: Hummingbirds maneuvered with highly repeatable performance.
source: We found that hummingbirds maneuvered with highly repeatable performance (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by the repeatability analysis presented in Figure 3.

claim: Maximum weight lifted during load lifting trials predicted most of the performance metrics that were measured, independent of a bird's wing size and shape.
source: Maximum weight lifted during load lifting trials predicted most of the performance metrics that we measured, independent of a bird's wing size and shape, such that birds with higher burst muscle capacity flew faster, had higher horizontal accelerations, faster rotations, and higher performance during complex turns (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 4.

claim: Aspect ratio predicted only two performance metrics: turns with higher centripetal acceleration and a greater percentage of arcing turns.
source: Aspect ratio predicted only two performance metrics, such that birds with higher aspect ratio wings performed turns with higher centripetal acceleration and a greater percentage of arcing turns (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: When flying in the presence of a competitor, hummingbirds used faster pitch velocities, although they used slower horizontal accelerations and decelerations.
source: When flying in the presence of a competitor, hummingbirds used faster pitch velocities, although they used slower horizontal accelerations and decelerations.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: During competition trials birds increased the proportion of arcing turns used.
source: During competition trials birds also increased the proportion of arcing turns used (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis presented in Figure 6.

claim: Burst muscle capacity is a much more important predictor of flight maneuverability than within-species variation in body mass, wing morphology, and competition with conspecifics.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that burst muscle capacity is a much more important predictor of flight maneuverability than within-species variation in body mass, wing morphology, and competition with conspecifics.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the collective results of the study.

claim: Wing loading was initially thought to be a key predictor of hummingbird flight performance and behavioral ecology.
source: For example, wing loading (the ratio of body mass to wing area or to area swept by the wings) was initially thought to be a key predictor of hummingbird flight performance and behavioral ecology (Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975; Feinsinger, 1976; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Feinsinger et al., 1979).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feinsinger and Chaplin, 1975; Feinsinger, 1976; Feinsinger and Colwell, 1978; Feinsinger et al., 1979.

claim: The hypothesis that wing size and body mass together determine maneuvering performance was not supported for any performance metric.
source: However, in our analysis the hypothesis that wing size and body mass together determine maneuvering performance was not supported for any performance metric (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by the model analysis presented in Supplementary file 1.

claim: It is possible that other morphological traits may determine maneuvering performance, or that subtle relationships may have gone undetected, because the analysis was limited to 20 individuals of a single species.
source: It is possible that other morphological traits may determine maneuvering performance, or that subtle relationships may have gone undetected, because our analysis was limited to 20 individuals of a single species.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning about the limitations of the study.

claim: Almost all of the performance metrics were highly repeatable, which indicates a potential role for intrinsic influences of wing morphology in determining maneuverability.
source: Almost all of the performance metrics were highly repeatable, which indicates a potential role for intrinsic influences of wing morphology in determining maneuverability.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the repeatability results.

claim: Aspect ratio is a key determinant in wing efficiency for fixed wings, such as during gliding.
source: Aspect ratio is a key determinant in wing efficiency for fixed wings, such as during gliding (Pennycuick, 1983), and it has recently been demonstrated that higher aspect ratio wings correspond to higher power factors in the revolving wings of hummingbirds (Kruyt et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Pennycuick, 1983.

claim: Higher aspect ratio wings correspond to higher power factors in the revolving wings of hummingbirds.
source: Aspect ratio is a key determinant in wing efficiency for fixed wings, such as during gliding (Pennycuick, 1983), and it has recently been demonstrated that higher aspect ratio wings correspond to higher power factors in the revolving wings of hummingbirds (Kruyt et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kruyt et al., 2014.

claim: Aspect ratio had a strong effect on the few performance metrics that it predicted, but did not affect most features of maneuvering performance.
source: We found that aspect ratio had a strong effect on the few performance metrics that it predicted, but did not affect most features of maneuvering performance.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis.

claim: The limited role of aspect ratio suggests a limited role for aerodynamic efficiency in many features of maneuvering.
source: This suggests a limited role for aerodynamic efficiency in many features of maneuvering.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the limited effect of aspect ratio.

claim: Burst muscle capacity predicted most of the performance metrics independently of any association with wing size or shape.
source: Burst muscle capacity predicted most of the performance metrics we considered, independently of any association with wing size or shape.
evidence: The claim is supported by the data analysis.

claim: Load lifting is measured as a transient escape maneuver that is likely anaerobic and performed inefficiently.
source: Load lifting is measured as a transient escape maneuver that is likely anaerobic and performed inefficiently.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge about the load lifting assay.

claim: All hummingbirds reach maximum load lifting performance at a geometric limit set by the amplitude of the wings: wing stroke amplitude cannot extend much past 180° without the two wings interfering with each other physically and aerodynamically.
source: All hummingbirds reach maximum load lifting performance at a geometric limit set by the amplitude of the wings: wing stroke amplitude cannot extend much past 180° without the two wings interfering with each other physically and aerodynamically (Chai and Dudley, 1995; Chai et al., 1997; Chai and Millard, 1997; Altshuler and Dudley, 2003).
